## The question

Is there a BMI threshold beyond which medical insurance charges increase more quickly, and does that pattern differ for smokers versus nonsmokers? This matters to healthcare analysts and insurers trying to understand what actually drives cost variation; so not just whether BMI matters, but *how* it matters.

We used the [Medical Insurance Costs dataset](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/mirichoi0218/insurance) from Kaggle. Each row is one person. There are 1,338 observations and seven variables: charges (in dollars), age, sex, BMI, children, smoker, and region. The original data collection process and the exact meaning of "charges" aren't clearly documented, so we can't make causal claims and the sample may not represent the broader population.

## What the baseline shows

**[Analysis coming — this section will be completed before the final submission.]**

```{r}
# Load packages and data, fit the baseline model.
library(tidyverse)
insurance <- read.csv("../insurance.csv")
base_model <- lm(charges ~ bmi + smoker + age, data = insurance)
round(coef(summary(base_model)), 2)
round(confint(base_model), 2)
```

```{r}
ggplot(insurance, aes(x = bmi, y = charges, color = smoker)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.35) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("no" = "#0072B2", "yes" = "#D55E00")) +
  labs(
    title = "BMI and Medical Insurance Charges by Smoking Status",
    x = "BMI (kg/m²)",
    y = "Medical insurance charges ($)",
    color = "Smoker"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```
